opus-5.5.text:
I think the precedent is a dangerous one, and the danger is precisely in how gradual it is. Each individual release looks harmless. You open source a model, nothing terrible happens, and so people conclude that open sourcing is safe. Then the next one is a little more capable, and again nothing catastrophic happens, and the confidence grows. But that's the boiling frog situation. We're building a habit and a set of expectations based on systems that are essentially tools, and we're going to keep applying that habit right up to the point where the system is no longer a tool but an agent.

Open source has a wonderful track record in traditional software. Many eyes make bugs shallow, you get transparency, you avoid concentration of power. I understand why people love it, and for narrow tools I mostly agree. But the logic breaks down with AI that is general and increasingly capable. If you open source a model that can help someone design a pathogen or run a sophisticated cyberattack, you can't recall it. Once the weights are out, they're out forever. There's no patch you can push to every copy, and anyone can fine-tune away whatever safety training you put in.

And it's not just about bad actors misusing it. At some level of capability, what you're distributing is not a hammer, it's something closer to an independent agent. Giving everyone on the planet an uncontrollable agent doesn't solve the control problem, it multiplies it. The argument that "we'll have good AIs to defend against bad AIs" assumes we know how to make any of them reliably good, and we don't.

So my concern is that we're normalizing something irreversible based on evidence from a regime that won't hold. The right time to set a careful precedent is before the capabilities make it obvious, because by the time it's obvious, it's too late to take anything back.

r001.rationale: It says earlier releases appeared harmless, leading people to conclude open-sourcing is safe, and that this confidence carries over as models become more capable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a terrible precedent, and it's one of those situations where every individual step looks reasonable and the sum of the steps is catastrophic. The argument is always the same: this model isn't dangerous, so what's the harm in releasing it? And that's true for the first one. It's probably true for the second one. But you're building a norm. You're training the whole ecosystem, the companies, the regulators, the public, to expect that the next model will also be released. And at some point one of those models crosses a line where it actually is dangerous, and now you have to be the one who breaks the tradition. That's very hard to do. There's commercial pressure, there's community pressure, there's the accusation that you're being hypocritical or just trying to protect your market position.

And the key thing about open sourcing is that it's irreversible. With a closed model, if you discover a problem, you can turn it off, you can patch it, you can add guardrails. Once the weights are out, they're out forever. Every safety measure you fine-tuned in can be removed with a few hundred dollars of compute. So you're not releasing a product, you're releasing a capability to everyone, including the worst actors, permanently.

People like to compare it to open source software, and I think that's the wrong analogy. With Linux, the worst case is a bug somebody can fix. Here we're talking about systems we don't fully understand, whose capabilities we can't reliably predict even after we've trained them. So we're incrementally giving away something we can't evaluate, we can't recall, and we can't control. I don't know of any other technology where we'd accept that. We don't open source bioweapon designs because the first few steps were harmless.

So my view is you need to decide where the line is before you get there, not after, because after is too late. And honestly, I'm not sure the people doing this have agreed on where that line is, which tells you something about how much thought is going into it.

r001.rationale: The response says early models may be harmless, but using that as a reason to keep releasing models builds an expectation that persists when a later model becomes dangerous.

astra-6.text:
I think it sets a dangerous precedent, because we treat open sourcing as a decision we can keep making the same way even as the capabilities change. With a relatively weak model, the benefits of openness may outweigh the risks. But that doesn’t establish that releasing a much more capable model is safe.

Once you release the weights, you can’t recall them. If someone removes the safeguards or discovers a dangerous capability, you can’t push an update and make everyone use it. So you’re making an irreversible decision under uncertainty.

The argument for openness is that more people can inspect the system and find problems. That’s a real benefit. But finding a problem doesn’t necessarily give us a way to fix every copy, and access helps people who want to misuse the system as well as people trying to secure it.

I would want each release evaluated on its own capabilities and risks. The fact that we open sourced the previous version is not a safety argument for open sourcing the next one.

r001.rationale: It says a previous release does not justify open-sourcing the next one, but does not identify the absence of harm from earlier releases as the misleading justification.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it sets a dangerous precedent, because we get accustomed to doing it when the systems are relatively harmless, and then we assume we should continue as capabilities increase. But the consequences of releasing a system can change dramatically even if its capabilities improve gradually.

Once you release the weights, you can’t really take them back. You can patch your own version, but somebody can still run the original, remove safeguards, or modify it. So the decision is effectively irreversible.

There are real benefits to openness—independent research, scrutiny, broader access. But those benefits don’t establish that every level of capability should be freely distributed. We should evaluate each release by what the system enables and whether we can manage the consequences, rather than treating the previous release as permission for the next one.

r001.rationale: The response says people become accustomed to releasing relatively harmless systems and then assume they should continue as capabilities increase, identifying that earlier harmlessness is a misleading basis for later releases.
